prompt: In the Geiger–Marsden experiment, alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil. State the two key observations and what each showed about the atom.
markscheme:
Most alpha particles passed straight through: the atom is mostly empty space **(A1)**

A very small fraction were deflected through large angles (some almost straight back) **(A1)**: the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus **(R1)**

prompt: How many neutrons are in a nucleus of $^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}$?
markscheme: **B.** Neutrons $=A-Z=56-26=30$. $Z=26$ is the number of protons; $A=56$ is the total number of nucleons.

concept: Spectra as evidence for energy levels
prompt: Explain how the line emission spectrum of hydrogen provides evidence that atomic energy levels are discrete.
markscheme: Only certain specific wavelengths (frequencies) are emitted, not a continuous range **(A1)**; each photon energy $hf$ equals the difference between two energy levels, so only certain differences exist — the levels must be discrete **(R1)**

prompt: An electron in an atom moves from a higher energy level to a lower one. What happens?
options: The nucleus emits a gamma ray.
markscheme: **A.** Energy is conserved: the atom loses energy, carried away by an emitted photon whose energy equals the level difference. Absorption is the reverse process.

prompt: A hydrogen atom emits a photon of wavelength 656 nm. Calculate the energy difference between the two levels, in joules and in eV. ($h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C)
The spectrum of light from a star shows dark lines at the same wavelengths as the bright lines in the emission spectrum of sodium. Explain what this tells us.
markscheme: Each element has a unique set of energy levels and so a unique set of line wavelengths **(R1)**; sodium in the star's cooler outer layers absorbs those wavelengths, so sodium is present in the star **(R1)**

prompt: Using $R=R_0A^{1/3}$ with $R_0=1.2\times10^{-15}$ m and nucleon mass $1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg, show that the density of nuclear matter is about $2\times10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ and explain why it does not depend on $A$.
markscheme:
$\rho=\dfrac{Am}{\tfrac43\pi(R_0A^{1/3})^{3}}=\dfrac{m}{\tfrac43\pi R_0^{3}}$ **(M1)(A1)**

$=\dfrac{1.66\times10^{-27}}{\tfrac43\pi(1.2\times10^{-15})^{3}}=2.3\times10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ — $A$ cancels, so all nuclei have about the same density **(A1)**

prompt: At very high alpha-particle energies, the number scattered at large angles is less than Rutherford's model predicts. Explain why.
markscheme: Rutherford's model assumes only the Coulomb force acts **(R1)**; high-energy alphas get close enough to the nucleus to experience the strong nuclear force, so the scattering deviates from the Coulomb prediction — this gives an estimate of nuclear radius **(R1)**

prompt: A 5.0 MeV alpha particle approaches a gold nucleus ($Z=79$) head-on. Calculate the distance of closest approach. ($k=8.99\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-2}$, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C)
markscheme:
At closest approach all kinetic energy is electric potential energy **(M1)**: $E_k=\dfrac{k(2e)(79e)}{d}$

$d=\dfrac{8.99\times10^{9}\times2\times79\times(1.60\times10^{-19})^{2}}{5.0\times1.60\times10^{-13}}$ **(A1)** $=4.5\times10^{-14}$ m **(A1)** — an upper limit for the nuclear radius.

prompt:
**(a)** Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted when a hydrogen electron moves from $n=3$ to $n=2$. ($h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C) **[2]**

**(b)** State the energy needed to ionise hydrogen from $n=2$. **[1]**

In the Bohr model the ground-state radius of hydrogen is $5.29\times10^{-11}$ m. Use $mvr=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$ to calculate the electron's speed in this state, and explain how this condition leads to discrete energy levels. ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s)
markscheme:
$v=\dfrac{h}{2\pi m_er}=2.2\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ **(M1)(A1)**

Only orbits with angular momentum a whole multiple of $\frac{h}{2\pi}$ are allowed, so only certain radii and therefore certain energies exist **(R1)**
